sources.title: 'I Play Rocky' Star Anthony Ippolito Filmed His Own Audition Before He Even Had the Script
sources.speaker: Anthony Ippolito, interviewed by Casey Loving (TheWrap)
sources.locator: Article body, paragraphs 3-6 (audition tape) and 8-9 (Gleason's Gym training)
sources.excerpt: "I hung a heavy bag in my grandma's basement. I didn't have a script, so I was just working with my imagination, trying to capture the physicality of the character," ... "It kind of felt like a bit of a long shot, but it was a creative exercise, and it was actually really fun." ... "It didn't seem very plausible to some people at the time, but I was really, really enthusiastic about it." ... "We were in Gleason's Gym, beating the crap out of each other. We got banged up. I had some wrist stuff, he had something with his ankle. It's not an easy game, but it was great." ... "I had seen an article that they were making this movie, and I had known a little bit of Stallone's story, so I was like, 'This is going to be a great movie,' and I really wanted to be a part of it. It didn't seem very plausible to some people at the time, but I was really, really enthusiastic about it,"
sources.context: Interview at TheWrap's studio at TIFF 2026. TheWrap reports he heard about the project from a news article, shot the tape with a friend who is an aspiring director and his cousin, his agent sent it to the producers and casting director, they sent the script back and asked for a proper audition, and he shot several more scenes on his own before being cast. He researched Stallone's 1972-1976 bit parts. 'He' in the gym quote is Stephan James (Carl Weathers). TheWrap also summarizes the film: it "centers on Stallone's adamant belief that he not only serve as the writer on 'Rocky' but also be the one to play the character, despite being turned down numerous times." The Gleason's Gym quote describes fight training with Stephan James for the shoot.

sources.title: 'I Play Rocky' Star Anthony Ippolito on Becoming Sylvester Stallone and Acting With a Dog: 'He Wasn't a Huge Fan of Me'
sources.speaker: Anthony Ippolito, interviewed by Marc Malkin (Variety)

sources.excerpt: "It had its moments for sure. I was being tested," ... "It's like a consistency thing, though. I had a great deal of time, so just an entire lifestyle shift and it was just one of the priorities of every day for a pretty long period." ... "They didn't necessarily know I was doing the prep, and they were like, 'What's going on here?' I was like, 'I've been going to the gym, been eating.'" ... The family question was 'What did family and friends think?' The patience line is about the dog playing Butkus on his first shooting day.

sources.title: 'I Play Rocky' star Anthony Ippolito on the "weight of responsibility" playing a young Sylvester Stallone
sources.speaker: Anthony Ippolito and Peter Farrelly, reported by Gabriele Niola (Screen Daily)
sources.locator: Rome Film Fest press conference report, full article
sources.excerpt: "There was a lot of intimidation at the beginning," ... "I was a fan of the movies and a fan of the character, and I understand how many people are, so I did feel the weight of the responsibility. But like any other situation, you just start by researching as much as you can." Farrelly: "He was the first person we looked at, the only person," ... "When I saw it, I said, 'That's it, search is over.' I didn't care if he'd ever been in anything else." Ippolito on Stallone: "He did feel very much like a lone wolf, kind of like an orphan in life in a lot of ways," ... "It was a very emotional shoot, and taxing in that way, but also very physically taxing." ... "He had so much going against him and he persevered through so much. His endurance, I think, radiates through Rocky." ... I Play Rocky charts the making of 1976's Rocky, which a then-unknown Stallone wrote and refused to sell unless he could play the lead.
sources.context: Press conference at the 21st Rome Film Fest, where he received the Progressive Award. Reports: Farrelly learned only in pre-production that Ippolito had played Pacino; Ippolito spent more than a year studying Stallone's interviews; he spoke to Stallone about a month before shooting; 34-day shoot; November scenes in cold New Jersey and Philadelphia warehouses left him 'pretty sick'; film was runner-up for TIFF's People's Choice Award; Amazon MGM opens it in select US cinemas on November 6.

sources.title: 'The Offer's' Anthony Ippolito on Being Intimidated to Play Al Pacino: 'It Makes You Want to Throw Up'
sources.speaker: Anthony Ippolito, quoted by Carson Burton (Variety)
sources.locator: Los Angeles premiere red-carpet report, final paragraphs
sources.excerpt: Anthony Ippolito, who plays Al Pacino, admitted playing the acting icon was "super intimidating." "It's pretty terrifying, it makes you want to throw up," he told Variety. "But it's also a freaking honor, and it's one of the coolest things that I've done as an actor. And it made me feel a huge weight of responsibility, but I had so much fun."
sources.context: Red-carpet quotes at The Offer's Los Angeles premiere, alongside Colin Hanks and Matthew Goode. Short answers to a standard question about playing an icon. The same article says The Offer follows producer Albert S. Ruddy, "played by Miles Teller".

sources.title: 'Rocky' Found: Anthony Ippolito to Play Sylvester Stallone in Amazon MGM's Movie Behind Making of Boxing Classic (Exclusive)
sources.speaker: Borys Kit (The Hollywood Reporter)
sources.locator: Casting exclusive, paragraphs 1-5 and closing credits paragraph
sources.excerpt: In a fitting echo of that spirit, Ippolito is said to have pursued the part of Stallone with the same relentless drive. Upon first hearing about the project, he made an unsolicited audition tape on his own and sent it directly to the producers. ... Ippolito will star as a young Sylvester Stallone in the drama, the true Hollywood story about an unknown actor with an unshakable belief that he wasn't just meant to write Rocky—he was meant to be Rocky Balboa. Told "no" at every turn, Stallone bets everything on himself, holding the line on playing the lead against seemingly impossible odds. ... He also co-starred in Netflix's romantic drama Purple Hearts, played a younger version of Adam Sandler's character in Pixels and appeared in David Chase's Not Fade Away.
sources.context: Casting announcement. Lists prior credits (The Offer as Pacino, Purple Hearts, young Sam Brenner in Pixels, Not Fade Away). The 'relentless drive' framing is the trade's and the studio's, not his own words. "That spirit" refers to the preceding sentence about Stallone betting everything on himself. The same story says Farrelly "won an Oscar for directing The Green Book"; Green Book's Oscars were Best Picture and Original Screenplay, so that wording is not used.

sources.title: Meet the cast of Netflix's gritty new NYC high school drama 'Grand Army'
sources.speaker: Anthony Ippolito, quoted by Chuck Arnold (New York Post)
sources.locator: Ippolito entry in the cast round-up ('Lucky break' and 'Advice to his high-school self')
sources.excerpt: "When I booked 'Grand Army,' I was playing for the Baruch [College] baseball team too. I broke my hand in a game, and my audition was scheduled a day after the procedure I ended up having, so I emailed my agent like, 'Listen, I'm gonna have to take a pass on this.' And my agent emailed me back, 'How would you feel about sending in a tape?' But I kept my hand out of the frame 'cause I didn't want them to see I had a broken hand." ... "I would tell myself, 'Stop being so hard on yourself, man.' High school's a tough place."
sources.context: Cast round-up for Grand Army's premiere. The Post calls him a '20-year-old Long Islander' who 'made his TV debut as a baseball-throwing toddler' and lists West Islip High School. On his character George: "Obviously, there's some of me in there... I was just drawing on my experiences with those guys."

sources.title: 'The Offer' Casting Director John Papsidera on Finding 'The Godfather' Stars
sources.speaker: John Papsidera (casting director, The Offer), from an interview with Below the Line

sources.title: Exclusive Interview: Pop Culturalist Chats with Grand Army's Anthony Ippolito
sources.speaker: Anthony Ippolito, interviewed by Pop-Culturalist
sources.locator: Q&A, questions 1-5 and 7 (question 1: how he discovered acting)
sources.excerpt: "When I was younger, I was on a bunch of news shows for baseball, and I got hooked up with an agent through that." ... "So many things—it takes a village. My mother pursued acting back in the day and always looks back on the memories she made on stage so fondly. My coach, Lynette Sheldon, has been a huge mentor for me on this journey and I'm forever grateful to her." ... "I could tell she was committed to authenticity and truth. In an industry where so much of the contrary exists, I felt so grateful to be a part of this." ... "A little bit, but I felt so strongly about the material that it was more of an excited energy than a nervous one. The biggest takeaway for me was the true value in being an ensemble member." ... sources.title: 'Grand Army's Anthony Ippolito: George 'Knows He Did Something Wrong' When It Comes To Joey's Assault
sources.speaker: Anthony Ippolito, interviewed by HollywoodLife
sources.locator: Q&A, first two answers (baseball and acting) and the answer on filming the assault scene
sources.excerpt: "I always kind of juggle the two. They were my two biggest passions in my life... if I was playing a baseball game, and I had an audition or we had a practice, I'd go to my coach and be like, listen, I've got to miss this practice. I've got to go to this audition. Or if we were playing in a championship game, and I had a commercial audition, I would tell my agent, please, I have a championship game." ... "I was trying to do everything. I was auditioning, doing school assignments from professors, studying for exams, taking acting classes and scene study classes in lower Manhattan, working with a coach, and auditioning. It was a lot." ... "my whole person was just completely making sure Odessa felt safe and comfortable throughout everything." ... Q: "As an actor, what did you do to create a safe space, not only for yourself but especially for Odessa A'Zion while you were filming such an intense scene?" A: "I think the answer is kind of right there. As an actor, it's your duty to tell the story as honestly and as truthfully as possible." ... "I broke my hand on the baseball field playing for Baruch, so I was out for the season after that. But like a week after that, I ended up booking Grand Army."
sources.context: Opened via a Wayback Machine raw copy because hollywoodlife.com blocks automated access. Long-form interview about Grand Army, including his character's sexual assault of a friend (a fictional storyline). Also says he broke his hand playing for Baruch and booked Grand Army about a week later, and that 'it's your duty to tell the story as honestly and as truthfully as possible.' HollywoodLife summarizes the storyline: Joey is raped by two of her best friends, George and Luke, in the back of a cab (fiction).

claims.claim: Before casting began on I Play Rocky, Ippolito hung a heavy bag in his grandmother's basement and taped himself as Stallone.
claims.passage: Before anyone had cast a movie about the making of _Rocky_, Anthony Ippolito hung a heavy bag in his grandmother's basement and started turning himself into Sylvester Stallone.
claims.inference: Hook. The basement and heavy bag are his own words to TheWrap (S01); 'before anyone had cast' rests on Farrelly's 'we hadn't even started casting' (S15) and Variety's premiere report (S22). 'Turning himself into' is the article's phrase for taping an impression, not a claim about the later physical transformation.
claims.alternative: Farrelly placed the taping in Ippolito's own apartment in one account (S16); the basement appears in Ippolito's account and Farrelly's other two.

claims.claim: Ippolito learned about I Play Rocky from a news article and taped himself as Stallone before anyone asked, initially without a script, using a heavy bag hung in his grandmother's basement, with a friend and his cousin; after producers sent the script he taped more scenes on his own.
claims.passage: "I didn't have a script, so I was just working with my imagination, trying to capture the physicality of the character," he told
claims.inference: Establishes the central observed choice of his career: an unsolicited, self-funded bid for a lead role. It shows initiative under long odds; it does not by itself show the motive.
claims.alternative: Self-taping is standard practice for working actors since 2020; agents routinely forward unsolicited tapes. The novelty is acting before casting began, which THR and the studio also used as a marketing story (S05 'relentless drive').

claims.claim: He learned of the project from a news article about Peter Farrelly, the director of Green Book, making the film.
claims.passage: He had read a news article saying Peter Farrelly, the director of _Green Book_, was making the film.
claims.inference: TheWrap (S01) and Collider (S20) have him learning of the film from an article; Rotten Tomatoes (S23) and Variety (S22) identify Farrelly as the Green Book filmmaker. The friend, cousin and agent steps stay in C01's claim but are no longer in the prose.
claims.alternative: Farrelly's Oscars for Green Book were for Best Picture and Original Screenplay; the article says only that he directed it.

claims.claim: Farrelly recalls that the studio asked how he would find a Stallone before casting began, and that he answered, 'He found us.'
claims.passage: but wanted to know how he would ever find a Stallone when casting hadn't even started. "I said, he found us."
claims.inference: Director's account at THR's TIFF studio (S15 10:07-10:14, captions and Whisper agree). Supports that the tape reached the filmmakers unsolicited.
claims.alternative: A polished premiere anecdote that compresses the agent and casting-director steps.

claims.claim: I Play Rocky premiered at TIFF on 2026-09-12 and was scheduled to open in limited US release on 2026-11-06, expanding nationwide on 2026-11-20.
claims.passage: The film premiered at TIFF on September 12, 2026, and was scheduled to open in limited U.S. release on November 6, 2026, expanding nationwide on November 20
claims.inference: Dates the moment readers are searching. The article's insight should not depend on these events.
claims.alternative: Earlier announcements gave 2026-11-13 for the limited release (moved up a week, S26); blue News gives 2026-11-26 for Switzerland.
claims.review_trigger: After 2026-11-20, confirm the release happened as scheduled and update box office or awards results (Golden Globe, SAG/Actor, Oscar nominations) only if they change how the article frames his career.

claims.claim: Variety's Clayton Davis called the performance 'a star-making turn.'
claims.passage: Variety's Clayton Davis called his performance "a star-making turn."
claims.inference: Critic's assessment, attributed by name; establishes why readers are searching now.
claims.alternative: Awards-advocacy framing from a premiere report (S22 context); other critics disagree (C34).

claims.claim: Birth date is unsettled: Wikipedia's infobox gives 1999-08-21 (consistent with 2025-2026 reported ages of 26 and 27), but Wikipedia's own category says 2000 births and 2020 and 2022 outlets called him 20 (October 2020) and 21 (May 2022), which imply 2000.
claims.passage: in his mid-to-late twenties as of 2026
claims.inference: Do not state a birth date or year. The 2020 and 2022 ages imply a birth between mid-May and mid-October 2000 (age 25 or 26 in September 2026); the Wikipedia infobox date gives 27. "Mid-to-late twenties as of 2026" is true under every report and is dated so it does not drift.
claims.alternative: The 2020-2022 outlets may have copied a wrong age; the 2026 trades may have copied Wikipedia.
claims.review_trigger: If he, his representatives or an official bio state his birth year, update the age wording and metadata and close this claim. In 2027 or later, keep the "as of 2026" anchor or restate the age from a settled birth year.

claims.claim: He is from Long Island (West Islip High School) and played baseball at Baruch College in Manhattan in 2019.
claims.passage: Ippolito is a Long Island native
claims.inference: Biographical orientation for the article; the Long Island and Baruch facts have independent sourcing.
claims.alternative: Wikipedia's 'only child of Anthony and Lorraine' detail lacks an adjacent citation and should not be used.

claims.claim: Before I Play Rocky he was a main-cast ensemble member of Netflix's Grand Army (2020), alongside Odessa A'Zion, and played a young Al Pacino in Paramount+'s The Offer (2022), which starred Miles Teller as producer Al Ruddy.
claims.passage: Before _I Play Rocky_ he had an ensemble role alongside [Odessa A'Zion](/personality-analysis/odessa-azion) on Netflix's _Grand Army_ (2020) and played a young Al Pacino in Paramount+'s _The Offer_ (2022), which starred [Miles Teller](/personality-analysis/miles-teller).
claims.inference: Supports the open-case framing: a long working career of small and supporting parts, with the first lead role arriving in 2026.
claims.alternative: Some outlets call Grand Army (2020) his breakout (S08), so 'unknown' overstates it; Variety's 'then-unknown' is the critic's phrase.

claims.claim: Some outlets call Grand Army his breakout; I Play Rocky is his first lead role.
claims.passage: Some outlets call _Grand Army_ his breakout. _I Play Rocky_ is his first lead.
claims.inference: Variety (S22), SCMP (S08) and Pop-Culturalist (S11) call Grand Army his breakout; his credits (S25, S05) show supporting, recurring or ensemble roles before this starring role. Stated plainly for the open-case eligibility question.
claims.alternative: Whether an ensemble lead on a Netflix series counts as a 'breakout' is a judgment call the verifier should weigh.

claims.claim: At The Offer's 2022 Los Angeles premiere he told Variety that playing Pacino was 'pretty terrifying, it makes you want to throw up.'
claims.passage: Playing Pacino was "pretty terrifying, it makes you want to throw up," he told
claims.inference: Fear and responsibility vocabulary recorded four years before the Stallone press tour, in a different role and outlet. Repetition across time is what lets it count as a pattern rather than one junket line.
claims.alternative: Every actor playing a living icon on a red carpet says some version of this; the situation, not a type, can explain it. In the same breath he said 'I had so much fun' and 'it's also a freaking honor'.

claims.claim: At the Rome Film Fest press conference (reported 2026-10-20) he said there was 'a lot of intimidation at the beginning'.
claims.passage: Playing Stallone brought "a lot of intimidation at the beginning," he said at the Rome Film Fest in October 2026
claims.inference: Fear vocabulary recorded four years after the Pacino quotes, in a different role and outlet.
claims.alternative: Press-conference humility from a newcomer on an Amazon MGM awards campaign is expected; the repeated phrase may be a stock answer.

claims.claim: The decisive move of his career, the I Play Rocky tape, was unsolicited, and he describes making it as fun.
claims.passage: Yet the move that made his career is one nobody invited, and he remembers making it as fun.
claims.inference: Summarizes C01/C42/C51: the tape preceded casting and was sent without a request (S05 "unsolicited"; S15 "we hadn't even started casting"), and he called making it "a creative exercise" that was "actually really fun" (S01).
claims.alternative: Self-taping is routine for working actors; the novelty is timing, and the studio has used the story in marketing.

claims.claim: Almost all of his public record is red-carpet remarks, festival junkets and short written Q&As.
claims.passage: As of October 2026, almost everything he has said in public comes from red carpets, festival junkets and short written Q&As.
claims.inference: Describes the opened record (2020-2026). HollywoodLife (S12) is the longest Q&A; no long-form profile or podcast was found on 2026-10-28 (research_tasks).
claims.alternative: A long-form interview may exist that research did not find; the claim is about sources opened as of 2026-10-28.
claims.review_trigger: Update when the first long-form interview, podcast, magazine profile or awards roundtable with him is published (expected after the 2026-11-06 and 2026-11-20 releases); then revise this sentence and the type answer.

claims.claim: Leading read: Type 6 at low confidence, with Type 3 nearly level and Types 9 and 1 live; in both icon roles he named the difficulty and answered it with research.
claims.passage: In both icon roles he named the difficulty and answered it with research.
claims.inference: The 60-word answer's evidential sentence. Pacino 2022: "trying to fill those shoes is kind of impossible" then old footage (S14). Stallone 2026: "intimidation" then "researching as much as you can" (S03), study of 1972-1976 bit parts (S18, S01).
claims.alternative: Research-after-fear is also ordinary actor preparation for any biographical role.

claims.claim: In 2022 and 2026 he names the difficulty of an icon role, then answers it with study.
claims.passage: The Six case is what he does with a daunting job, in 2022 and again in 2026: he names the difficulty, then studies until he has footing.
claims.inference: The repeated sequence the Six read rests on: difficulty named (S14 "kind of impossible"; S03 "intimidation"; S16 "I don't know how to do this ... daunting"), then research or step-by-step study (S14 old footage; S03 "researching as much as you can"; S16 "piece by piece"). Edit-stage correction: the draft's counterphobic "bold step anyway" clause is dropped because no source shows fear before the tape (C111).
claims.alternative: Naming difficulty and then researching is ordinary actor preparation for any biographical role, and a Three or One would do it too. Both instances are icon roles on promotional tours (C57).

claims.claim: Ippolito says the first tape was improvised without a script; TheWrap reports the producers then sent the script and asked for a proper audition, and he taped more scenes on his own.
claims.passage: The first tape was improvised: "It kind of felt like a bit of a long shot, but it was a creative exercise, and it was actually really fun." The producers then sent the script and asked for a proper audition, and he shot several more scenes on his own, TheWrap reports.
claims.inference: His first-person sequence, preferred over Farrelly's for the process (see C03). The quote is verbatim from TheWrap.
claims.alternative: The second step is TheWrap's paraphrase, not his words.

claims.claim: Details of the tape conflict: Ippolito says the first tape was made with no script and more scenes followed once producers sent it; Farrelly says he 'somehow found the script' and taped three scenes in his grandmother's basement (S15, S22) or 'in his own apartment' (S16).
claims.passage: Farrelly remembers it differently. At THR's studio he said Ippolito "had somehow found the script" and taped three scenes. In a September 2026 video for [IMDb](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TP7M9Ce7eUM), he placed the taping "in his own apartment." Both men agree the tape arrived before casting began.
claims.inference: Use Ippolito's first-person sequence for the process; attribute Farrelly's version as his recollection. The grandmother's basement appears in both Ippolito's and most of Farrelly's accounts.
claims.alternative: Both may be partly right (an early improvised tape, then three scripted scenes); Farrelly may only have seen the later tape.

claims.claim: Farrelly said at the Rome Film Fest that Ippolito was 'the first person we looked at, the only person'.
claims.passage: "He was the first person we looked at, the only person," Farrelly said in Rome.
claims.inference: Independent confirmation from the director that the self-generated tape, not a formal process, won the role.
claims.alternative: Director anecdotes told at premieres are polished for audiences; the casting director and agent steps are compressed.

claims.claim: Ippolito explains the bid: "at least if I was seen and I could present my interpretation, then I'd be able to live with it even if it didn't go my way. I just really had to try to get in the door."
claims.passage: I just really felt that at least if I was seen and I could present my interpretation, then I'd be able to live with it even if it didn't go my way. I just really had to try to get in the door.
claims.inference: The closest he comes in the record to naming what drove the risk. "Seen" and "get in the door" are ordinary casting language for getting an audition (C97). "Live with it even if it didn't go my way" names acceptance of losing as the payoff, which tilts slightly toward regret avoidance (C98) without excluding a visibility reading.
claims.alternative: Fillers ("like", "um") and a repeated "get in" are dropped; the captions put a period after "my way" while Whisper attaches "Even if it didn't go my way" to the next sentence. Either parse leaves the same meaning: he could accept not getting the part. One junket answer cannot separate 3, 6 or 1.

claims.claim: The 'seen' answer supports a visibility reading (3) or a regret-avoidance reading (6) and cannot separate them.
claims.passage: Read one way, the key word is "seen," the move of someone who needs the right people to notice. Read another, the key phrase is "live with it": he was guarding against regret.
claims.inference: Labels both readings of C04 as interpretation and states that one answer cannot decide them.
claims.alternative: "Seen" is also casting shop talk (C97), so the visibility reading rests on the act more than the word; "live with it" could also express an inner standard (Type 1) or simple pragmatism.

claims.claim: Asked whether he ever hesitated to take a role that means so much to people, he said he was fighting for it; Farrelly added that it wasn't much of a fight because they never considered anyone else after him.
claims.passage: "I was fighting for it," he said. Farrelly added: "By the way, it wasn't much of a fight. We never considered anyone else after him."
claims.inference: Farrelly's line is praise: the tape ended the search (S15 09:40-09:46, Whisper wording, fillers dropped). Edit-stage change: "cut in" replaced by neutral attribution, and the continuation added so the line reads as the compliment it was.
claims.alternative: Captions and Whisper record "No." and "No, I mean" before "I was fighting for it"; the speaker was not frame-checked, so it is not quoted. If it is his, it weighs against a fear-first reading. Whisper alone hears "I knew I could do it", which is not quoted.

claims.claim: In 2019, during his Baruch College baseball season, he broke his hand in a game the day before a Grand Army audition, emailed his agent to pass, then sent a self-tape at the agent's suggestion and kept the hand out of frame.
claims.passage: In 2019, playing baseball for Baruch College, he broke his hand in a game, and his _Grand Army_ audition fell the day after a procedure on it. "I emailed my agent like, 'Listen, I'm gonna have to take a pass on this,'" he told
claims.inference: Edit-stage correction: the injury and tape date to his 2019 Baruch season (S28 "played for the Bearcats in 2019"; S12 broke the hand playing for Baruch, "out for the season", booked Grand Army about a week later). 2020 is the year of the Post interview, which the prose keeps as the interview date. Here his first move was to withdraw and his agent prompted the tape.
claims.alternative: Hiding the cast is ordinary professional self-presentation. The Post and HollywoodLife timelines differ slightly (audition a day after the procedure vs booking about a week after the break).

claims.claim: The agent suggested a tape and he kept his broken hand out of the frame so the producers would not see it.
claims.passage: The agent suggested a tape. "But I kept my hand out of the frame 'cause I didn't want them to see I had a broken hand."
claims.inference: Self-presentation under adverse conditions; listed in the Type 3 case.
claims.alternative: Hiding an injury from a casting team is ordinary professional caution.

claims.claim: The broken hand explains why he first offered to pass in 2019; that tape was his agent's idea, while the I Play Rocky tape was his own.
claims.passage: The broken hand explains why he first offered to pass. Still, the contrast is real: in 2019 the tape was his agent's idea, and for _I Play Rocky_ it was his own.
claims.inference: Contrast between C06/C54 and C01, with the circumstantial explanation stated first. Year corrected to 2019 (S28, S12).
claims.alternative: One earlier instance only; the contrast may show circumstance (injury) rather than growth.

claims.claim: At the same 2022 premiere he called playing Pacino 'a freaking honor' that 'made me feel a huge weight of responsibility, but I had so much fun.'
claims.passage: Playing Pacino was also "a freaking honor," he told Variety, and it "made me feel a huge weight of responsibility, but I had so much fun."
claims.inference: First recorded use of 'weight of responsibility'; the fun and honor halves are kept so the fear line is not read alone.
claims.alternative: Stock red-carpet answer to a stock question about playing an icon.

claims.claim: To THR in 2022 he said he was 'kind of terrified of [him] seeing it' because he had looked up to Pacino.
claims.passage: "I'm kind of terrified of [him] seeing it because he's someone I've looked up to, and I respect his work."
claims.inference: Fear tied to a respected figure watching; the bracket is THR's.
claims.alternative: Any actor playing a living icon would say this.

claims.claim: In Rome (2026) he said he felt 'the weight of the responsibility' because so many people are fans, and that 'like any other situation, you just start by researching as much as you can.'
claims.passage: "I was a fan of the movies and a fan of the character, and I understand how many people are, so I did feel the weight of the responsibility. But like any other situation, you just start by researching as much as you can."
claims.inference: Same phrase as 2022 plus a stated general coping rule (research). Screen Daily prints it as one continuous quotation.
claims.alternative: Press-conference humility from a newcomer on an awards campaign; the phrase may be a stock answer.

claims.claim: Asked where he starts with Stallone's voice and posture, he said: 'You start by saying, I don't know how to do this, and it's daunting, but you have to kind of be humbled by the task and figure it out from there piece by piece.'
claims.passage: "You start by saying, I don't know how to do this, and it's daunting, but you have to kind of be humbled by the task and figure it out from there piece by piece."

type_hypothesis.against: The fear vocabulary that carries the reading is concentrated where almost any actor would feel it: playing living icons who might watch, on promotional tours where newcomer humility is expected, and in 2022 THR gave the whole Offer cast the 'Absolutely Terrifying' register (C99). Its object is being watched and judged by admired figures and fans, which is heart-triad territory as much as head-triad (C103). The dated order shows no fear before the I Play Rocky tape: before it came homework and enthusiasm ('actually really fun', 'really, really enthusiastic'), and the fear words followed casting (C111), so the draft's counterphobic reading is withdrawn. Outside the icon roles, in 2020, he described series-regular pressure as 'more of an excited energy than a nervous one' (C19), and his fear words come paired with honor, fun and gratitude (C85). The record shows no worst-case planning, testing of loyalty or wariness of authority (C66). His yearbook motto celebrates walking his own way (C23). The body transformation followed the tape at the production's direction (C87), so it counts for no type. No one who has known him beyond a single production has spoken on record (C75).
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: Type 3: the I Play Rocky tape is his defining move, and in 2019 he taped a scheduled audition with a broken hand kept out of frame (C38). Farrelly: 'Very Stallone-like in his approach to this. He just made it happen.' (C13). THR's casting story tied his pursuit to Stallone's bet on himself (C67), though that parallel is also the studio's marketing frame (C105). He ran a full athletic, academic and acting schedule ('I was trying to do everything', C07) and began acting to book commercials (C17). With an even press-tour discount, the humility evidence against Three (premiere thanks C35; Farrelly's post-hiring Pacino story C68) weakens, and what survives is small: his 2020 remark that life without acting would be 'pretty much the same' (C22) and the near-absence of winning language (C85). Six is listed first only on the tiebreaker in C89. Type 9 (receptive absorption, ensemble, enthusiasm for a story) and Type 1 (authenticity and duty language) are also live; Type 4 is named and set aside (C108).
type_hypothesis.discriminator: No defensible discriminator exists yet. The current tiebreaker is thin: he meets hard tasks by admitting he doesn't know how and studying piece by piece, and did the homework before the tape as for Pacino (C89, C90), which sits more naturally with Six than with an image-guarding Three, but it too is press-tour speech. What would separate them: his own unprompted, long-form account of what the tape was for and what steadied him (getting noticed and breaking through for 3; preparing until ready and not letting down people who trusted him for 6), his stated reasons for handling the imitation reviews and for choosing his next role, and testimony from people who have known him longer than one production.
type_hypothesis.unexplained: His yearbook motto, which both leading reads can only half claim; the private painting and music; the cheerful, easy manner reporters describe (S31); his 2020 remark that pressure felt like 'excited energy'; the reform-minded moral language around Grand Army; and how much of the humility and the fear talk is temperament versus a newcomer's press-tour script.

settle_signals: His own retelling of the tape. His answer so far is enthusiasm for a story that had inspired him (TheWrap, Collider, September 2026), which fits every reading. In long-form interviews after the November 2026 release, does he say it was about getting noticed (3), preparing until he felt ready and not letting down people who trusted him (6), joining a story he loved, win or lose (9), or owing Stallone an honest portrayal (1)?

His stated reasons, in a long-form or unscripted setting, for how he handled critics who call the performance imitation (TheWrap, Region Free): crediting results and momentum (3), working it through with people he trusts (6), not taking it in (9), or a principled defense of the craft choice (1). Gracious answers alone do not count; they are standard on an awards campaign.

The reason he gives for his next role, since offers and agents drive the bare choice: the size of the opportunity (3), trust in the people making it, such as Farrelly (6), the chance to disappear into an ensemble (9), or what the project gets right (1). If he frames it as self-expression or feeling different, reopen Type 4.

On-record testimony from people who have known him longer than one production (Grand Army's Katie Cappiello or cast, coach Lynette Sheldon, The Offer's cast): do they describe over-preparation and loyalty (6), relentless drive (3), easygoing going-along (9), or exacting standards and self-criticism (1)?
